Part I: Foundations of Mathematical Macroeconomics

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Connects to: Principles Parts I–II

This part builds the mathematical scaffolding that every subsequent part uses. Readers who have taken a year of calculus and a semester of linear algebra will find it a targeted review with macroeconomic applications — not a repetition of what they already know, but a reframing of familiar tools in the language of economic models. Each chapter introduces its tools in the context of a specific macroeconomic question, so that the mathematics never floats free of motivation.

Chapter 1 develops optimization theory — the mathematical heart of all macroeconomic modeling, since macroeconomics is the study of agents who optimize subject to constraints. Chapter 2 applies linear algebra to economic systems, deriving the Leontief inverse and the IS–LM solution as matrix problems. Chapters 3 and 4 develop differential and difference equations respectively, covering the analytical toolkit for the dynamic models of Parts III–IV. Chapter 5 introduces the stochastic processes — particularly the AR(1) — that appear as the shock processes in every model from Chapter 17 onward.

A note on difficulty: Chapter 1 through Chapter 5 are sequenced so that each builds on the previous, but they are also largely self-contained. A reader who wants only the stochastic methods of Part V can read Chapter 5 directly after Chapter 2.

Chapter 1: Calculus and Optimization in Macroeconomics¶

From Utility Maximization to Lagrange Multipliers

“Optimization is the heart of economics. Almost every economic model, at its core, is an optimization problem.” — Thomas Sargent

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 1 (scope of macroeconomics); Ch. 11 (consumption theory, Euler equation); Ch. 12 (investment theory, Tobin’s q); Ch. 13 (labour supply and demand) [P:Ch.1, P:Ch.11, P:Ch.12, P:Ch.13]

1.1 Why Calculus? The Optimization Imperative¶

Macroeconomics, at every level of sophistication, is a discipline about constrained choice. A household chooses a consumption path to maximize lifetime utility subject to a budget constraint. A firm chooses investment to maximize the present value of profits subject to an adjustment cost technology. A central bank chooses a path for the interest rate to minimize a loss function subject to the constraints imposed by the Phillips curve and the IS relationship. In each case, the economic content is carried by the optimization problem, and the calculus is the language in which that problem is solved.

The models of Principles frequently invoke optimization without deriving the conditions in full. Chapter 11 of Principles states the Euler equation u′(ct)=β(1+rt+1)Et[u′(ct+1)]u'(c_t) = \beta(1+r_{t+1})\mathbb{E}_t[u'(c_{t+1})]u′(ct​)=β(1+rt+1​)Et​[u′(ct+1​)] and then explains it verbally; this chapter derives it, together with every other first-order condition that appears in Principles, from the underlying optimization problem. The derivations are not decorative. They matter because:

  1. They reveal what assumptions the result depends on — and what happens when those assumptions are relaxed.

  2. They provide the algebraic form needed for numerical computation (Part VI).

  3. They are the basis for comparative statics — understanding how the equilibrium changes when parameters change.

We begin with unconstrained optimization, move to equality-constrained problems (the Lagrangian), then to inequality-constrained problems (Kuhn–Tucker conditions), and finally to the implicit function theorem, which turns comparative statics from a graphical exercise into an algebraic one.

1.2 Unconstrained Optimization¶

1.2.1 Single-Variable Problems¶

Definition 1.1 (Local and Global Maxima). Let f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R. A point x∗∈Rx^* \in \mathbb{R}x∗∈R is a local maximum of fff if there exists ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 such that f(x∗)≥f(x)f(x^*) \geq f(x)f(x∗)≥f(x) for all xxx with ∣x−x∗∣<ε|x - x^*| < \varepsilon∣x−x∗∣<ε. It is a global maximum if f(x∗)≥f(x)f(x^*) \geq f(x)f(x∗)≥f(x) for all x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R.

The fundamental result connecting calculus to optimization:

Theorem 1.1 (First-Order Necessary Condition). If fff is differentiable and x∗x^*x∗ is a local maximum (or minimum) of fff, then f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*) = 0f′(x∗)=0.

Proof sketch. If f′(x∗)>0f'(x^*) > 0f′(x∗)>0, then by continuity of f′f'f′ there exists δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that f′(x)>0f'(x) > 0f′(x)>0 for all x∈(x∗−δ,x∗+δ)x \in (x^* - \delta, x^* + \delta)x∈(x∗−δ,x∗+δ). Then fff is strictly increasing on this interval, so f(x∗+δ/2)>f(x∗)f(x^* + \delta/2) > f(x^*)f(x∗+δ/2)>f(x∗), contradicting x∗x^*x∗ being a local maximum. Similarly for f′(x∗)<0f'(x^*) < 0f′(x∗)<0. □\square□

The first-order condition (FOC) f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*) = 0f′(x∗)=0 is necessary but not sufficient. Points where f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 are called critical points or stationary points; they may be maxima, minima, or inflection points.

Theorem 1.2 (Second-Order Sufficient Conditions). Let fff be twice differentiable and let x∗x^*x∗ satisfy f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*) = 0f′(x∗)=0.

  • If f′′(x∗)<0f''(x^*) < 0f′′(x∗)<0, then x∗x^*x∗ is a strict local maximum.

  • If f′′(x∗)>0f''(x^*) > 0f′′(x∗)>0, then x∗x^*x∗ is a strict local minimum.

  • If f′′(x∗)=0f''(x^*) = 0f′′(x∗)=0, the test is inconclusive.

Application to macroeconomics: The Baumol–Tobin money demand model of Principles Ch. 14 minimizes total cost TC(n)=iY/(2n)+bnTC(n) = iY/(2n) + bnTC(n)=iY/(2n)+bn over the number of bank trips nnn. Setting TC′(n)=0TC'(n) = 0TC′(n)=0:

−iY2n2+b=0  ⟹  n∗=iY2b.-\frac{iY}{2n^2} + b = 0 \implies n^* = \sqrt{\frac{iY}{2b}}.−2n2iY​+b=0⟹n∗=2biY​​.
(1)

The second derivative TC′′(n)=iY/n3>0TC''(n) = iY/n^3 > 0TC′′(n)=iY/n3>0 confirms this is a minimum.

1.2.2 Multivariate Unconstrained Optimization¶

Let f:Rn→Rf: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}f:Rn→R. The gradient is:

∇f(x)=(∂f∂x1,∂f∂x2,…,∂f∂xn)′.\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right)'.∇f(x)=(∂x1​∂f​,∂x2​∂f​,…,∂xn​∂f​)′.
(2)

Theorem 1.3 (Multivariate FOC). If x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ is a local maximum or minimum of a differentiable f:Rn→Rf: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}f:Rn→R, then ∇f(x∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x∗)=0.

The second-order conditions require the Hessian matrix:

Hf(x)=(∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯⋮⋮⋱).H_f(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2} & \cdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2 \partial x_1} & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2^2} & \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{pmatrix}.Hf​(x)=⎝⎛​∂x12​∂2f​∂x2​∂x1​∂2f​⋮​∂x1​∂x2​∂2f​∂x22​∂2f​⋮​⋯⋯⋱​⎠⎞​.
(3)

By Young’s theorem (symmetry of mixed partials), HfH_fHf​ is symmetric.

Definition 1.2 (Positive and Negative Definite Matrices). A symmetric matrix AAA is positive definite if v′Av>0\mathbf{v}'A\mathbf{v} > 0v′Av>0 for all nonzero v∈Rn\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^nv∈Rn; equivalently, all eigenvalues of AAA are strictly positive. It is negative definite if v′Av<0\mathbf{v}'A\mathbf{v} < 0v′Av<0 for all nonzero v\mathbf{v}v; equivalently, all eigenvalues are strictly negative. It is indefinite if it has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Theorem 1.4 (Multivariate Second-Order Conditions). At a critical point x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗:

  • Hf(x∗)H_f(\mathbf{x}^*)Hf​(x∗) negative definite ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ strict local maximum.

  • Hf(x∗)H_f(\mathbf{x}^*)Hf​(x∗) positive definite ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ strict local minimum.

  • Hf(x∗)H_f(\mathbf{x}^*)Hf​(x∗) indefinite ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ saddle point.

A practical check for negative definiteness: the leading principal minors of −Hf-H_f−Hf​ must all be positive (i.e., HfH_fHf​ is negative definite iff −Hf-H_f−Hf​ is positive definite iff all leading principal minors of −Hf-H_f−Hf​ are positive).

1.2.3 The Envelope Theorem¶

The envelope theorem answers the question: how does the optimized value of the objective function change when a parameter changes, without re-solving the optimization problem?

Theorem 1.5 (Envelope Theorem, Unconstrained). Let f(x;α)f(x; \alpha)f(x;α) be differentiable in both xxx and the parameter α\alphaα. Define the value function V(α)=max⁡xf(x;α)V(\alpha) = \max_x f(x; \alpha)V(α)=maxx​f(x;α), with maximizer x∗(α)x^*(\alpha)x∗(α) (assuming it is differentiable in α\alphaα). Then:

dVdα=∂f(x∗(α);α)∂α.\frac{dV}{d\alpha} = \frac{\partial f(x^*(\alpha); \alpha)}{\partial \alpha}.dαdV​=∂α∂f(x∗(α);α)​.
(4)

That is, the total derivative of the value function with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the objective with respect to that parameter, evaluated at the optimum. The channel through which α\alphaα changes the optimal x∗x^*x∗ — the indirect effect — contributes nothing to the change in VVV because fx(x∗;α)=0f_x(x^*;\alpha) = 0fx​(x∗;α)=0 at the optimum.

Proof:

dVdα=ddαf(x∗(α);α)=fx(x∗(α);α)⏟=0 by FOC⋅dx∗dα+fα(x∗(α);α)=fα(x∗(α);α).□\frac{dV}{d\alpha} = \frac{d}{d\alpha} f(x^*(\alpha);\alpha) = \underbrace{f_x(x^*(\alpha);\alpha)}_{=0 \text{ by FOC}} \cdot \frac{dx^*}{d\alpha} + f_\alpha(x^*(\alpha);\alpha) = f_\alpha(x^*(\alpha);\alpha). \quad \squaredαdV​=dαd​f(x∗(α);α)==0 by FOCfx​(x∗(α);α)​​⋅dαdx∗​+fα​(x∗(α);α)=fα​(x∗(α);α).□
(5)

Application: In the firm’s investment problem of Principles Ch. 12, the Hamiltonian is the value function and the shadow price qtq_tqt​ (Tobin’s qqq) is the envelope of the profit function with respect to the capital stock. The costate equation q˙=rq−FK\dot{q} = rq - F_Kq˙​=rq−FK​ is the envelope theorem applied to the continuous-time optimal control problem — we derive this fully in Chapter 11.

1.3 Constrained Optimization: Equality Constraints¶

Most optimization problems in macroeconomics involve constraints. The household maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint; the firm maximizes profit subject to a production technology. Equality constraints are handled by the method of Lagrange multipliers.

1.3.1 The Lagrangian Method¶

Definition 1.3 (Lagrangian). For the problem max⁡xf(x)\max_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x})maxx​f(x) subject to g(x)=0g(\mathbf{x}) = 0g(x)=0, the Lagrangian function is:

L(x,λ)=f(x)−λ g(x),\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda\, g(\mathbf{x}),L(x,λ)=f(x)−λg(x),
(6)

where λ∈R\lambda \in \mathbb{R}λ∈R is the Lagrange multiplier or shadow price associated with the constraint.

Theorem 1.6 (Lagrange Necessary Conditions). If x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ is a local maximum of fff subject to g(x)=0g(\mathbf{x}) = 0g(x)=0, and if the constraint qualification ∇g(x∗)≠0\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^*) \neq \mathbf{0}∇g(x∗)=0 holds, then there exists λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ such that:

∇xL(x∗,λ∗)=0andg(x∗)=0.\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*, \lambda^*) = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{and} \quad g(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0.∇x​L(x∗,λ∗)=0andg(x∗)=0.
(7)

In components: ∂f/∂xi=λ∗∂g/∂xi\partial f/\partial x_i = \lambda^* \partial g/\partial x_i∂f/∂xi​=λ∗∂g/∂xi​ for all iii, plus the constraint.

Derivation from first principles. Consider max⁡x1,x2f(x1,x2)\max_{x_1, x_2} f(x_1, x_2)maxx1​,x2​​f(x1​,x2​) subject to g(x1,x2)=0g(x_1, x_2) = 0g(x1​,x2​)=0. Since the constraint implicitly defines x2x_2x2​ as a function of x1x_1x1​ near the optimum (by the IFT, provided gx2≠0g_{x_2} \neq 0gx2​​=0), we can write x2=h(x1)x_2 = h(x_1)x2​=h(x1​) where h′(x1)=−gx1/gx2h'(x_1) = -g_{x_1}/g_{x_2}h′(x1​)=−gx1​​/gx2​​. Substituting into the objective and taking the total derivative with respect to x1x_1x1​:

ddx1f(x1,h(x1))=fx1+fx2h′(x1)=fx1−fx2gx1gx2=0.\frac{d}{dx_1}f(x_1, h(x_1)) = f_{x_1} + f_{x_2} h'(x_1) = f_{x_1} - f_{x_2}\frac{g_{x_1}}{g_{x_2}} = 0.dx1​d​f(x1​,h(x1​))=fx1​​+fx2​​h′(x1​)=fx1​​−fx2​​gx2​​gx1​​​=0.
(8)

Rearranging: fx1/gx1=fx2/gx2≡λ∗f_{x_1}/g_{x_1} = f_{x_2}/g_{x_2} \equiv \lambda^*fx1​​/gx1​​=fx2​​/gx2​​≡λ∗. This gives fxi=λ∗gxif_{x_i} = \lambda^* g_{x_i}fxi​​=λ∗gxi​​ for i=1,2i=1,2i=1,2, which are exactly the FOCs of the Lagrangian. □\square□

1.3.2 Economic Interpretation of the Lagrange Multiplier¶

The Lagrange multiplier λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ measures the marginal value of relaxing the constraint. Formally, if the constraint is g(x)=cg(\mathbf{x}) = cg(x)=c (parameterized by ccc) and V(c)=max⁡x:g(x)=cf(x)V(c) = \max_{\mathbf{x}: g(\mathbf{x})=c} f(\mathbf{x})V(c)=maxx:g(x)=c​f(x), then dV/dc=λ∗dV/dc = \lambda^*dV/dc=λ∗. Each unit increase in ccc allows the agent to reach a higher objective by exactly λ∗\lambda^*λ∗.

In the household problem with budget constraint p1x1+p2x2=mp_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = mp1​x1​+p2​x2​=m, the Lagrange multiplier is the marginal utility of income: λ∗=dV/dm\lambda^* = dV/dmλ∗=dV/dm where V(m)V(m)V(m) is the indirect utility function. In the firm’s problem with a capital constraint, λ∗\lambda^*λ∗ is the shadow price of capital — Tobin’s qqq [P:Ch.12].

For max⁡f(x)\max f(\mathbf{x})maxf(x) subject to gj(x)=0g_j(\mathbf{x}) = 0gj​(x)=0, j=1,…,mj = 1, \ldots, mj=1,…,m (with m<nm < nm<n), the Lagrangian is:

L(x,λ)=f(x)−∑j=1mλjgj(x),\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j g_j(\mathbf{x}),L(x,λ)=f(x)−j=1∑m​λj​gj​(x),
(9)

and the FOCs are ∇xL=0\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}∇x​L=0 and gj(x)=0g_j(\mathbf{x}) = 0gj​(x)=0 for all jjj, giving n+mn + mn+m equations in n+mn + mn+m unknowns.

Worked Example 1.1: Household Utility Maximization

A household maximizes u(c1,c2)=c11−σ/(1−σ)+βc21−σ/(1−σ)u(c_1, c_2) = c_1^{1-\sigma}/(1-\sigma) + \beta c_2^{1-\sigma}/(1-\sigma)u(c1​,c2​)=c11−σ​/(1−σ)+βc21−σ​/(1−σ) subject to c1+c2/(1+r)=wc_1 + c_2/(1+r) = wc1​+c2​/(1+r)=w, where β∈(0,1)\beta \in (0,1)β∈(0,1), σ>0\sigma > 0σ>0, and www is lifetime wealth. L=c11−σ1−σ+βc21−σ1−σ−λ(c1+c21+r−w).\mathcal{L} = \frac{c_1^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta\frac{c_2^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} - \lambda\left(c_1 + \frac{c_2}{1+r} - w\right).L=1−σc11−σ​​+β1−σc21−σ​​−λ(c1​+1+rc2​​−w).

(12)

Equating: c1−σ=β(1+r)c2−σc_1^{-\sigma} = \beta(1+r) c_2^{-\sigma}c1−σ​=β(1+r)c2−σ​, which gives the Euler equation:

c2c1=[β(1+r)]1/σ.\frac{c_2}{c_1} = [\beta(1+r)]^{1/\sigma}.c1​c2​​=[β(1+r)]1/σ.

1.4 Constrained Optimization: Inequality Constraints¶

When constraints may or may not bind at the optimum — as in the borrowing constraint of Principles Ch. 11.4 — the Kuhn–Tucker conditions replace the simple Lagrange conditions.

1.4.1 The Kuhn–Tucker Conditions¶

Theorem 1.7 (Kuhn–Tucker Necessary Conditions). Consider max⁡xf(x)\max_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x})maxx​f(x) subject to gj(x)≤0g_j(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0gj​(x)≤0 for j=1,…,mj = 1, \ldots, mj=1,…,m. Define the Lagrangian L(x,μ)=f(x)−∑jμjgj(x)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\mu}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \sum_j \mu_j g_j(\mathbf{x})L(x,μ)=f(x)−∑j​μj​gj​(x). If x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ is a local maximum and a constraint qualification holds, then there exist μj∗≥0\mu_j^* \geq 0μj∗​≥0 such that:

  1. Stationarity: ∇xL(x∗,μ∗)=0\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*, \boldsymbol{\mu}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇x​L(x∗,μ∗)=0

  2. Primal feasibility: gj(x∗)≤0g_j(\mathbf{x}^*) \leq 0gj​(x∗)≤0 for all jjj

  3. Dual feasibility: μj∗≥0\mu_j^* \geq 0μj∗​≥0 for all jjj

  4. Complementary slackness: μj∗gj(x∗)=0\mu_j^* g_j(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0μj∗​gj​(x∗)=0 for all jjj

The complementary slackness condition is the key: either the constraint is binding (gj(x∗)=0g_j(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0gj​(x∗)=0) or the multiplier is zero (μj∗=0\mu_j^* = 0μj∗​=0), or both. If a constraint is not binding, it plays no role in the optimum.

Application to the liquidity-constrained consumer [P:Ch.11.4]: The household maximizes u(ct)+βE[u(ct+1)]u(c_t) + \beta\mathbb{E}[u(c_{t+1})]u(ct​)+βE[u(ct+1​)] subject to at+1=(1+r)(at+yt−ct)a_{t+1} = (1+r)(a_t + y_t - c_t)at+1​=(1+r)(at​+yt​−ct​) and the borrowing constraint at+1≥b‾a_{t+1} \geq \underline{b}at+1​≥b​. Writing the constraint as −at+1+b‾≤0-a_{t+1} + \underline{b} \leq 0−at+1​+b​≤0, the KKT conditions add a multiplier μt≥0\mu_t \geq 0μt​≥0:

u′(ct)=β(1+r)E[u′(ct+1)]+μt,μt(at+1−b‾)=0.u'(c_t) = \beta(1+r)\mathbb{E}[u'(c_{t+1})] + \mu_t, \quad \mu_t(a_{t+1} - \underline{b}) = 0.u′(ct​)=β(1+r)E[u′(ct+1​)]+μt​,μt​(at+1​−b​)=0.
(15)

When the constraint binds (at+1=b‾a_{t+1} = \underline{b}at+1​=b​): μt=u′(ct)−β(1+r)E[u′(ct+1)]>0\mu_t = u'(c_t) - \beta(1+r)\mathbb{E}[u'(c_{t+1})] > 0μt​=u′(ct​)−β(1+r)E[u′(ct+1​)]>0 — the household is “constrained” in the sense that the Euler equation holds with a positive wedge. When the constraint is slack: μt=0\mu_t = 0μt​=0 and the standard Euler equation holds. This is the formal derivation of Principles equation (11.16).

1.5 The Implicit Function Theorem and Comparative Statics¶

Comparative statics asks: when a parameter changes, how does the equilibrium change? The implicit function theorem (IFT) provides the algebraic tool for answering this question systematically.

Theorem 1.8 (Implicit Function Theorem — Scalar Version). Let F(x,α):R2→RF(x, \alpha): \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}F(x,α):R2→R be continuously differentiable. Suppose F(x∗,α∗)=0F(x^*, \alpha^*) = 0F(x∗,α∗)=0 and Fx(x∗,α∗)≠0F_x(x^*, \alpha^*) \neq 0Fx​(x∗,α∗)=0. Then there exists a neighborhood of α∗\alpha^*α∗ and a unique continuously differentiable function x=x(α)x = x(\alpha)x=x(α) such that x(α∗)=x∗x(\alpha^*) = x^*x(α∗)=x∗ and F(x(α),α)=0F(x(\alpha), \alpha) = 0F(x(α),α)=0. Moreover:

dx∗dα=−Fα(x∗,α∗)Fx(x∗,α∗).\frac{dx^*}{d\alpha} = -\frac{F_\alpha(x^*, \alpha^*)}{F_x(x^*, \alpha^*)}.dαdx∗​=−Fx​(x∗,α∗)Fα​(x∗,α∗)​.
(16)

The multivariate version: if F(x,α)=0\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \mathbf{0}F(x,α)=0 defines x\mathbf{x}x implicitly as a function of α\boldsymbol{\alpha}α near (x∗,α∗)(\mathbf{x}^*, \boldsymbol{\alpha}^*)(x∗,α∗), and if the Jacobian ∂F/∂x\partial\mathbf{F}/\partial\mathbf{x}∂F/∂x is nonsingular at (x∗,α∗)(\mathbf{x}^*, \boldsymbol{\alpha}^*)(x∗,α∗), then:

dx∗dα=−(∂F∂x)−1∂F∂α.\frac{d\mathbf{x}^*}{d\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = -\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.dαdx∗​=−(∂x∂F​)−1∂α∂F​.
(17)

This is the fundamental formula for comparative statics in any system of equilibrium conditions.

Worked Example 1.2: Comparative Statics for the IS Curve

Derive the slope of the IS curve (how YYY changes with rrr in goods-market equilibrium) using the IFT.

The IS curve is the locus satisfying F(Y,r)≡Y−C(Y−T)−I(r)−G=0F(Y, r) \equiv Y - C(Y - T) - I(r) - G = 0F(Y,r)≡Y−C(Y−T)−I(r)−G=0. Then:

FY=1−C′(Y−T),Fr=−I′(r).F_Y = 1 - C'(Y - T), \quad F_r = -I'(r).FY​=1−C′(Y−T),Fr​=−I′(r).
(18)

By the IFT:

dYdr∣IS=−FrFY=−−I′(r)1−C′=I′(r)1−C′<0,\left.\frac{dY}{dr}\right|_{\text{IS}} = -\frac{F_r}{F_Y} = -\frac{-I'(r)}{1 - C'} = \frac{I'(r)}{1 - C'} < 0,drdY​∣∣​IS​=−FY​Fr​​=−1−C′−I′(r)​=1−C′I′(r)​<0,
(19)

since I′(r)<0I'(r) < 0I′(r)<0 and 1−C′>01 - C' > 01−C′>0. The IS curve slopes downward, with steeper slope when the MPC C′C'C′ is large (strong multiplier) or investment is insensitive to the interest rate (small ∣I′∣|I'|∣I′∣). This is the algebraic derivation of the IS slope stated qualitatively in Principles Ch. 9.1 [P:Ch.9.1]. □\square□

1.6 Concavity, Convexity, and Global Optima¶

The FOCs and SOCs identify local optima. For global optima, we need concavity or convexity.

Definition 1.4 (Concave and Convex Functions). A function f:C→Rf: C \to \mathbb{R}f:C→R defined on a convex set C⊆RnC \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nC⊆Rn is concave if for all x,y∈C\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in Cx,y∈C and θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0,1]θ∈[0,1]:

f(θx+(1−θ)y)≥θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y).f(\theta\mathbf{x} + (1-\theta)\mathbf{y}) \geq \theta f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-\theta) f(\mathbf{y}).f(θx+(1−θ)y)≥θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y).
(20)

It is strictly concave if the inequality is strict for x≠y\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{y}x=y and θ∈(0,1)\theta \in (0,1)θ∈(0,1).

Proposition 1.1. If fff is strictly concave, any local maximum is also a global maximum. If fff is twice differentiable, it is concave iff HfH_fHf​ is negative semi-definite everywhere.

Most utility functions used in macroeconomics are strictly concave: u(c)=ln⁡cu(c) = \ln cu(c)=lnc, u(c)=c1−σ/(1−σ)u(c) = c^{1-\sigma}/(1-\sigma)u(c)=c1−σ/(1−σ) for σ>0\sigma > 0σ>0, and u(c)=−(c−c∗)2u(c) = -(c - c^*)^2u(c)=−(c−c∗)2 are all strictly concave in ccc. This guarantees that the Lagrange FOCs identify a global maximum.

For convex constraint sets (which are the rule in consumer and producer theory), the constraint qualification is automatically satisfied, and the Lagrange/KKT conditions are both necessary and sufficient under concavity of the objective.

1.7 Worked Example: Deriving the Labour Supply Curve¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 13 (labour supply and demand) [P:Ch.13.1]

Consider a household with preferences u(c,ℓ)=ln⁡c+χln⁡ℓu(c, \ell) = \ln c + \chi \ln \ellu(c,ℓ)=lnc+χlnℓ, where ccc is consumption and ℓ=1−n\ell = 1 - nℓ=1−n is leisure (nnn is hours worked), and χ>0\chi > 0χ>0 is the relative weight on leisure. The budget constraint is c=wn+ac = w n + ac=wn+a (wage income plus non-labour income aaa), and time is normalized so ℓ+n=1\ell + n = 1ℓ+n=1.

Step 1: Write the constrained problem.

max⁡c,nln⁡c+χln⁡(1−n)s.t.c=wn+a.\max_{c, n} \ln c + \chi \ln(1-n) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad c = wn + a.c,nmax​lnc+χln(1−n)s.t.c=wn+a.
(21)

Substitute the constraint: max⁡nln⁡(wn+a)+χln⁡(1−n)\max_n \ln(wn + a) + \chi\ln(1-n)maxn​ln(wn+a)+χln(1−n).

Step 2: First-order condition.

ddn[ln⁡(wn+a)+χln⁡(1−n)]=wwn+a−χ1−n=0.\frac{d}{dn}\left[\ln(wn+a) + \chi\ln(1-n)\right] = \frac{w}{wn+a} - \frac{\chi}{1-n} = 0.dnd​[ln(wn+a)+χln(1−n)]=wn+aw​−1−nχ​=0.
(22)

Step 3: Solve for n∗n^*n∗.

w(1−n)=χ(wn+a)  ⟹  w−wn=χwn+χa  ⟹  n∗(w,a)=w−χaw(1+χ).w(1-n) = \chi(wn+a) \implies w - wn = \chi wn + \chi a \implies n^*(w,a) = \frac{w - \chi a}{w(1+\chi)}.w(1−n)=χ(wn+a)⟹w−wn=χwn+χa⟹n∗(w,a)=w(1+χ)w−χa​.
(23)

Step 4: Comparative statics.

∂n∗∂w=11+χ+χaw2(1+χ)>0(substitution effect dominates for a>0).\frac{\partial n^*}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{1+\chi} + \frac{\chi a}{w^2(1+\chi)} > 0 \quad \text{(substitution effect dominates for } a > 0\text{)}.∂w∂n∗​=1+χ1​+w2(1+χ)χa​>0(substitution effect dominates for a>0).
(24)
∂n∗∂a=−χw(1+χ)<0(labour supply falls with non-labour income).\frac{\partial n^*}{\partial a} = \frac{-\chi}{w(1+\chi)} < 0 \quad \text{(labour supply falls with non-labour income)}.∂a∂n∗​=w(1+χ)−χ​<0(labour supply falls with non-labour income).
(25)

Step 5: Verify second-order condition.

d2dn2[ln⁡(wn+a)+χln⁡(1−n)]=−w2(wn+a)2−χ(1−n)2<0.\frac{d^2}{dn^2}\left[\ln(wn+a)+\chi\ln(1-n)\right] = -\frac{w^2}{(wn+a)^2} - \frac{\chi}{(1-n)^2} < 0.dn2d2​[ln(wn+a)+χln(1−n)]=−(wn+a)2w2​−(1−n)2χ​<0.
(26)

The objective is strictly concave in nnn, confirming n∗n^*n∗ is a global maximum.

The upward-sloping labour supply curve (∂n∗/∂w>0\partial n^*/\partial w > 0∂n∗/∂w>0) is consistent with the competitive benchmark of Principles Ch. 13.1 [P:Ch.13.1]. The formula n∗=(w−χa)/[w(1+χ)]n^* = (w - \chi a)/[w(1+\chi)]n∗=(w−χa)/[w(1+χ)] also shows that the Frisch elasticity of labour supply (the elasticity of nnn with respect to www holding the marginal utility of wealth constant) depends on the preference parameter χ\chiχ — a result used in Chapter 13 of this volume when calibrating the RBC model.

Note the idiom f ⍣ converged ⊢ start: apply f repeatedly until the predicate converged is satisfied. ⍣ with a dyadic right argument iterates until convergence — this pattern appears throughout the book for fixed-point computations.

Exercise 1.2 (Python)¶

# Python — Newton's method for critical point of f(x) = -x**4 + 3*x**3 - 2
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
import numpy as np

f   = lambda x: -x**4 + 3*x**3 - 2
df  = lambda x: -4*x**3 + 9*x**2    # first derivative
ddf = lambda x: -12*x**2 + 18*x     # second derivative

def newton_critical(x0, tol=1e-10, max_iter=100):
    x = x0
    for i in range(max_iter):
        x_new = x - df(x) / ddf(x)
        if abs(x_new - x) < tol:
            return x_new, i+1
        x = x_new
    raise RuntimeError("Did not converge")

x_star, iters = newton_critical(0.5)
print(f"x* = {x_star:.10f}, f(x*) = {f(x_star):.10f}, converged in {iters} iterations")
x* = 0.0000000001, f(x*) = -2.0000000000, converged in 32 iterations

Exercise 1.3 (Julia)¶

# Julia — Newton's method for critical point
f(x)   = -x^4 + 3x^3 - 2
df(x)  = -4x^3 + 9x^2
ddf(x) = -12x^2 + 18x

function newton_critical(x0; tol=1e-10, max_iter=100)
    x = x0
    for i in 1:max_iter
        x_new = x - df(x) / ddf(x)
        abs(x_new - x) < tol && return x_new, i
        x = x_new
    end
    error("Did not converge")
end

x_star, iters = newton_critical(0.5)
println("x* = $(round(x_star, digits=10)),  f(x*) = $(round(f(x_star), digits=10)),  iters = $iters")

Exercise 1.4 (R)¶

# R — Newton's method for critical point
f   <- function(x) -x^4 + 3*x^3 - 2
df  <- function(x) -4*x^3 + 9*x^2
ddf <- function(x) -12*x^2 + 18*x

newton_critical <- function(x0, tol = 1e-10, max_iter = 100) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    x_new <- x - df(x) / ddf(x)
    if (abs(x_new - x) < tol) return(list(x = x_new, iters = i))
    x <- x_new
  }
  stop("Did not converge")
}

res <- newton_critical(0.5)
cat(sprintf("x* = %.10f,  f(x*) = %.10f,  iters = %d\n", res$x, f(res$x), res$iters))

1.9 Chapter Summary¶

This chapter developed the optimization tools that underlie every macroeconomic model in Principles and in this volume.

Key results:

  • The first-order necessary condition ∇f(x∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}∇f(x∗)=0 must hold at any interior maximum or minimum of a differentiable function.

  • The second-order sufficient condition requires the Hessian to be negative definite (for a maximum) or positive definite (for a minimum) at the critical point.

  • The envelope theorem states that the marginal value of a parameter equals its direct effect on the objective, evaluated at the optimum; indirect effects through the optimal policy function contribute nothing.

  • The Lagrange method converts equality-constrained problems into unconstrained problems over an augmented objective; the multiplier is the shadow price of the constraint.

  • The Kuhn–Tucker conditions extend the Lagrange method to inequality constraints, with complementary slackness ensuring that a slack constraint has a zero multiplier.

  • The implicit function theorem provides the formula for comparative statics: dx∗/dα=−(Fx)−1Fαd\mathbf{x}^*/d\boldsymbol{\alpha} = -(F_{\mathbf{x}})^{-1} F_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}dx∗/dα=−(Fx​)−1Fα​.

Connections forward: Chapter 3 extends these tools to infinite-horizon continuous-time problems (the Hamiltonians of optimal control). Chapter 11 applies them to the RCK model. Chapter 15 develops the discrete-time analogue (Bellman equations and dynamic programming). Chapter 18 applies the Lagrange method to the household’s problem under rational expectations.
